Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: • We propose marginal attention as a relevant quantity to study in language models. Aggregated over heads, it is shared across unrelated models. Per head, it is specific to each model. • We connect attention statistics in language models to the input-output Jacobian, and show that model smoothness and next-token distribution similarity alone are theoretically sufficient for input-output Jacobian near-identifiability across models ( Theorem 1 ). • We show that per-head marginal attention is a stable quantity across documents, enabling efficient KV cache eviction via a one-time, document-agnostic head budget calculation. Recently, a considerable body of work has examined the similarity of representations across independently trained models, including large language models (LLMs). These works propose similarity metrics ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ; Raghu et al., 2017 ; Morcos et al., 2018 ) , compose models ( Lenc & Vedaldi, 2015 ; Bansal et al., 2021 ; Norelli et al., 2023 ; Maiorca et al., 2023 ) , or study the geometry of the representation space ( Moschella et al., 2023 ; Huh et al., 2024 ) . Here, we shift the focus from representation-level to the mechanics that produce these representations, the interactions between data inside the model. In transformer-based language models this is largely determined by the attention mechanism and, as the next paragraph reviews, attention itself is not identifiable across models. In our work, we propose a marginal version of attention whose per-token reduction is a property of the text, shared and conserved across models. Attention compared across models. The attention mechanism is the core component of transformer-based models. On one hand, when treated as a free parameter, the attention matrix has been shown to be non-identifiable ( Brunner et al., 2020 ) , and specific heads are generally not empirically identifiable across models ( Xu, 2026 ; Paulo & Belrose, 2026 ) , perhaps owing to their differing specializations ( Voita et al., 2019 ; Michel et al., 2019 ; Gandelsman et al., 2024 ; Basile et al., 2025a ; Basile et al., 2025b ) . On the other hand, summary statistics of attention maps have been observed to be well-conserved across models, with Liang et al. (2025) first noting that they can be sufficient to differentiate documents visually. Other work exploits the emergent property of attention that it approximates the computational map for explanations ( Abnar & Zuidema, 2020 ) and model provenance assessment ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, we show that marginal attention approximates the input–output Jacobian and prove that models with similar next-token predictions have similar Jacobians, which provides insight into why the per-token marginal attention is near-identifiable across models. KV cache eviction. Attention has a well-known quadratic cost in the input length, and at inference this cost is paid in memory as well. Serving a long context requires storing the key and value vectors of every past token for every head. An active line of work, eviction, bounds that memory by keeping only a subset of positions inside a fixed budget, while alternatives compress every position instead ( Monteiro et al., 2026 ) or learn a compact cache for a document by distillation ( Laguna et al., 2026 ) . Most eviction methods rank positions by the attention they have received, keeping the sinks and a recent window ( Xiao et al., 2024 ) , the most attended positions ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Adnan et al., 2024 ; Chari & Durme, 2025 ) , or those the current query attends to ( Li et al., 2024b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . A more recent line of works ranks a position by the attention it will receive, estimated from the queries seen so far ( Devoto et al., 2025 ) , computed on a reconstruction pass ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , predicted by a trained surrogate ( Jegou & Jeblick, 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) , or learned directly as a policy over future utility ( Moschella et al., 2026 ) . Head budgets follow from the observation that a few specialised heads perform long-context retrieval ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , so heads are labelled offline as retrieval or streaming ( Xiao et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) , reallocated within a layer ( Feng et al., 2025 ) or over depth ( Cai et al., 2025 ) , or assigned a static table solved on a calibration context ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . A smaller model of the same family has also been used in place of the target, by transplanting its attention ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) or lending its scores ( Zhao et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2026 ) , only within a family; the cache itself has also been translated between models with trained maps ( Dery et al., 2026 ; Castin et al., 2026 ) . In this work, we build on the per-head marginal attention to obtain a static head budget for eviction, and on the identifiability of marginal attention to adjust the token scorer with a smaller model. 3 Marginal attention Notation. Spearman correlation between per-head profiles; 67 models, 170 documents. The per-token profile is indexed by the document’s positions, so we compare it across models; the per-head profile is indexed by the model’s heads, so we compare it across documents. We ask whether each reduction is a property of the text, shared across models, or a property of the model, stable across documents. In the following, we first define the two reductions ( Definitions 2 and 3 ), show that the first is a property of the text and the second a property of the model ( Section 3.1 ), then explain the first theoretically through the Jacobian ( Section 4 ), and finally use the second as a key-value cache budget ( Section 5 ). 3.1 The two reductions across models and across documents We now empirically test whether the per-token marginal attention ( Definition 2 ) is shared across models and the per-head marginal attention ( Definition 3 ) is stable across documents. Experimental setting. We compute both reductions on one set of models and documents, and compare each along two axes: across models on the same document, and across documents within the same model. We consider 67 open models from 38 families and 28 architectures, from 0.27B to 117B parameters, trained by different labs on different data with different tokenizers, including mixture-of-experts and multi-head-latent-attention models. We use 850 natural documents, 50 from each of 17 domains of the Pile ( Gao et al., 2020 ) ; the per-head comparison uses 170 of them, a seeded subsample of 10 per domain. Tokenizers differ, so for the per-token profile we broadcast each token’s value to the characters it covers, and compare two profiles per document by Spearman correlation after removing the average over 50 relative-position bins. Heads of different models have no correspondence, so we average each per-head profile over documents and bin it into ten relative-depth bins before comparing two models; within one model we compare the profile averaged over one half of the documents with the profile averaged over the other half, on the same ten bins, and the profile of one document with the average over all the others, on the full vector over heads. As a reference for the per-token profile, we compare each model with the consensus on a different document. We also show the agreement between ten pythia-410m reruns that differ only in the pretraining seed. As a reference for the per-head profile, we permute each model’s heads. Details are in Appendices A , B and C . Result analysis. Figures 2 and 3 (left) show the main comparison for each reduction. Across models, the agreement of each model’s per-token profile with the consensus of the other models is high (0.87), and its agreement with the consensus on a different document is near zero (0.02), so the agreement is specific to the document. Deleting punctuation and whitespace from the axis raises this agreement slightly, so it does not come from delimiters ( Table 5 ), and neither the number of models in the consensus nor the head weights change it much ( Appendix B ). Across documents, the per-head profile one model computes on one half of the documents agrees closely with the profile it computes on the other half (0.99), and between models of different architectures agreement is much lower (0.37) on the same ten depth bins, so the profile is specific to the model. The right panels group model pairs by what they have in common; both profiles agree most between a model and a version trained from it and least between unrelated models ( Sections B.1 and C ). Takeaway. These results show that the per-token marginal attention is a model-agnostic property of the text, and the per-head marginal attention is a document-agnostic property of the model. 4 Identifiability in the marginal attention In this section, we explain the stability of per-token marginal attention across models. We start with an empirical observation: across models, the per-token marginal attention is reliably correlated with an analogous statistic of the input-output Jacobian .
